who is not happy or satisfied with something. The word "sentiment" comes from the Latin sentire, meaning to feel.
The term sentimentality has been used in a pejorative sense since at least 1830 and refers specifically to an excessive emotionalism that can be seen as artificial rather than genuine; it may also refer more generally to any excess of emotion (see hyperbole). Sentiments are often associated with women's writing because they were considered appropriate for female authors but inappropriate for male ones.[1]
Sentimental literature

Sentiment Analysis (SA) refers to techniques for automatically identifying opinions expressed about entities such as people , products , organizations etc., within text . The goal of SA systems is usually twofold: first identify positive vs negative sentiments ; secondly classify these expressions according to polarity .
In this paper I will focus only one aspect - detecting negativity -, which may be considered more challenging than other tasks because it requires dealing not only with words but also phrases containing multiple negations ("not", "no"...) followed immediately after another word expressing positivity e.g.: “I don't think you should go there.” In order to detect whether someone feels negatively toward some entity mentioned earlier sentence must contain at least three consecutive tokens separated either side-by-side (“don’t” +“think”) OR following eachother sequentially(‘do’+ ‘n’t’)
